client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away two months ago — it was so sudden, and I just wasn't prepared for it at all. Everything feels kind of gray now, like I go through the motions of my day but nothing really feels meaningful or enjoyable anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because I don't see how words can change the fact that he's just... gone.
therapist: What you're carrying right now — the sudden loss, the grayness, the sense of just going through the motions — that's an enormous weight, and it makes complete sense that you'd feel uncertain about whether anything could help. I notice there's something quiet and heavy in the way you're sharing this, almost like part of you is holding back, maybe exhausted or even a little numb beneath the words. I'm wondering — when you say you don't see how talking could help, is there a part of you that *wants* it to, even just a little, or does it feel more like hope itself has gone quiet right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... maybe there's a tiny part of me that wants it to help, otherwise I wouldn't be sitting here. But it feels almost embarrassing to admit that, like if I let myself hope and it doesn't work, I'll just feel worse than before. It's like hope itself feels dangerous right now, not just quiet.
therapist: That insight — that you're here *because* some part of you hasn't given up — is actually really significant, and it took courage to say it out loud. What you're describing, where hope feels risky rather than comforting, makes a lot of sense after a loss that came without warning, because your sense of safety got shattered too. I'm curious — has that feeling, that it's safer not to hope, shown up in other parts of your life since he passed, or does it feel mostly tied to this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, it's definitely spread into other areas... like, I used to make plans with friends pretty easily, but now I find myself always holding back, not committing to things, because some part of me is waiting for it to fall apart anyway. It's like I stopped letting myself look forward to anything. I hadn't really connected that to losing him until just now, but when you say it like that, it makes a strange kind of sense.
therapist: That moment of connection you just made — linking the pulling back from friends to losing your dad — is really meaningful, and it sounds like something just shifted a little for you in recognizing that. There's something I notice in how you're speaking though, a softness and a kind of quiet heaviness that makes me wonder if this realization brings some sadness with it, not just clarity. What's coming up for you right now as you sit with that connection?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, there is sadness. I think I've been so focused on just getting through each day that I haven't really let myself feel how much I miss him, and now that I've said it out loud, it's sitting in my chest in a way that's hard to ignore. It's like I've been keeping everyone at a distance because some part of me is scared that if I let people in again, I'll just lose them too.
therapist: What you just named — that the distance you've been keeping isn't really about people, it's about protecting yourself from another loss — that's a profound and tender thing to recognize. It makes so much sense that your mind found that way to keep you safe, even if it's also been keeping you lonely. I want to gently ask: when you imagine actually letting someone in, even just a little, what feels most scary about that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think what scares me most is that I'll let someone in, actually trust them, and then they'll leave anyway — or I'll do something to push them away without even meaning to. It's like... I almost expect it to go wrong, so why even start? And then I'd have to go through that whole cycle of loss again, which honestly feels unbearable to even think about.
therapist: The fear you're describing — that closeness inevitably leads to loss, and that you might even be the one to cause it — is such a painful place to be, like you're caught between longing for connection and bracing for the hurt you're certain will follow. What strikes me is that this belief, that it will go wrong, feels less like a prediction and more like something loss has *taught* you, even if it's not the whole truth. I'm wondering — before you lost your dad, did relationships feel this fragile to you, or is this a new lens that grief has put over everything?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, that question kind of stopped me in my tracks, because no... before my dad died, I don't think I walked around waiting for things to fall apart. I had friends I felt close to, I wasn't constantly second-guessing whether people actually wanted me around. It's like grief just... rewired something, and now I can't remember how to be with people without this low hum of dread underneath it all.
therapist: What you just recognized is really important — that this dread isn't *you*, it's something grief layered on top of a person who actually knew how to connect and trust. There's something quietly painful in the way you're sitting with that, like you're mourning not just your dad but also this easier version of yourself that felt safer in the world. I wonder — does it feel like that person is gone, or more like they've just gone quiet under the weight of all of this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think... gone quiet feels more right than gone, actually. Like that version of me is still in there somewhere, but buried under so much heaviness that I can't really access them anymore. It's strange to even think about it that way, because part of me has just assumed for so long that this is who I am now, that the grief just rewired me permanently.
therapist: The fact that "gone quiet" feels more true than "gone" is actually a really hopeful sign, even if it doesn't feel that way yet — it means some part of you knows that person is still there, waiting. But I notice that even as you're saying something that carries a little hope, there's a kind of exhaustion underneath it, like the words are moving faster than the feeling, almost as if you're working hard to hold something together right now. What's actually happening inside you as you say this — is there something that wants to slow down, or even surface?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, you're right that there's exhaustion there, and I didn't even realize how much until you named it just now. It's like I've been holding my breath for so long, waiting for things to go back to normal with my friend, that I forgot I was even doing it. I think what wants to surface is this fear that if I stop holding it together, I'll have to actually admit that I don't know if things will ever be the same between us.
therapist: That fear — that things might never go back to the way they were with your friend — sounds like it carries a lot of grief all on its own, almost like a second loss sitting alongside losing your dad. And there's something I notice in how quickly and intently you're speaking right now, like this has been pressing against the surface for a while and finally found a way out. I'm wondering — what would it mean for you if things between you and your friend *did* change, even if they changed in a different way than before rather than going back to exactly what they were?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think you're right that it's been pressing on me — I didn't even realize how much until just now, saying it out loud. But when you ask what it would mean if things changed in a different way... I don't know, that almost feels scarier than losing the friendship entirely, like a version of him that I don't fully recognize anymore. Because so much of who I was before my dad died is tied up in how he knew me, and if that shifts, it's like losing another piece of the person I used to be.
therapist: What you just said — that your friend knowing the "old you" feels like a living connection to who you were before — that's such a tender and important thing to name, because it means this friendship carries a weight far beyond just companionship right now. It's like he's become a kind of keeper of the person you're afraid of losing, and the thought of that shifting feels like grief on top of grief. I'm sitting with you in that — and I want to gently ask: is there any part of you that has actually talked to him about any of this, or has the fear of things changing kept you from letting him see where you really are?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: No, I haven't told him any of this. Every time I think about bringing it up, I get this wave of anxiety like... what if saying it out loud makes it real, or worse, what if he doesn't understand and I lose even the version of the friendship I have now? So I just keep showing up, acting like things are fine, and then going home feeling more alone than before I saw him.
therapist: The cycle you're describing — showing up, holding it all in, and leaving feeling more alone — sounds exhausting and quietly heartbreaking, like you're working so hard to protect the friendship that you're slowly losing yourself inside of it. What strikes me is that the very thing you're afraid of, being truly seen and possibly misunderstood, is actually the only thing that could break that loneliness you feel when you walk away. I'm curious — when you imagine your friend sitting across from you and actually *understanding*, even just a little, what does that feel like to picture?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
